questions.question: Why does liver disease require medication-specific assessment?
choices: It can alter drug exposure, bleeding risk, toxicity, and tolerance of adverse effects
It affects only bilirubin values
It makes all medications ineffective
It eliminates the need for interaction review
questions.explanation: The liver is central to metabolism and synthetic function. Medication safety in liver disease requires clinical context, not a single laboratory result.

questions.question: What is the safest initial approach to suspected drug-induced liver injury?
choices: Obtain a complete exposure timeline and evaluate medication, supplement, alcohol, viral, obstructive, and other causes while assessing severity
Assume every abnormal liver test is caused by the newest prescription
Tell the patient to ignore jaundice until the next visit
Stop every medication without considering withdrawal or disease risk
questions.explanation: DILI is a diagnosis requiring careful timeline and differential assessment. Severe symptoms or jaundice require timely evaluation and coordinated medication decisions.

questions.question: Which statement about chronic hepatitis B is most accurate?
choices: Treatment and monitoring are individualized; not every patient needs antiviral medication, but chronic infection needs appropriate longitudinal expert care
Every person with HBV needs the same medication immediately
HBV medication can be stopped whenever symptoms improve
Acute and chronic HBV are managed identically
questions.explanation: Chronic HBV decisions depend on viral activity, liver disease, co-infections, pregnancy, and other factors. Expert longitudinal management is recommended.

questions.question: What is a key medication-safety concern in HIV/HBV coinfection?
choices: Stopping agents active against HBV during ART changes can cause serious hepatocellular injury from reactivation hepatitis
ART has no relevance to HBV
HBV status is unimportant before changing ART
A partial medication stop is always safer than consultation
questions.explanation: Some ART components are active against HBV. Regimen changes in HIV/HBV coinfection require deliberate coordination to avoid HBV reactivation injury.

questions.question: What is the best statement about HCV direct-acting antiviral therapy?
choices: It can cure most HCV infections, but medication interactions and liver-stage assessment must be reviewed before treatment
It should be started without any medication review
A positive HCV antibody alone always proves active infection
It eliminates all future liver follow-up for every patient
questions.explanation: DAAs are highly effective, but active infection confirmation, chronic liver assessment, HBV/HIV testing, and interaction review are essential.

questions.question: Why should an acid-reducing medication be reviewed before starting a patient on an HCV DAA regimen?
choices: Some DAA regimens have clinically meaningful interactions with acid-reducing agents
Acid-reducing medicines cure HCV
They eliminate the need for liver monitoring
They have identical effects with every antiviral
questions.explanation: Drug interaction effects are regimen specific. Check the exact DAA and acid-reducing product using a current interaction resource.

questions.question: Which presentation in a patient with cirrhosis most strongly supports emergency evaluation?
choices: New confusion, gastrointestinal bleeding, hypotension, severe jaundice, or rapidly worsening condition
A stable preventive-care question
A routine refill request without symptoms
A mild chronic symptom already evaluated by hepatology
questions.explanation: Encephalopathy, major bleeding, instability, and decompensation symptoms can be life threatening and require urgent assessment.

questions.question: Why should an FNP ask specifically about over-the-counter medications and supplements in a patient with abnormal liver tests?
choices: They can cause hepatotoxicity, duplication, contamination, or interactions even when marketed as natural
Only prescriptions can affect the liver
Supplements do not need to be documented
Alcohol history is more important than every other exposure
questions.explanation: A complete exposure history includes prescription drugs, acetaminophen combinations, supplements, herbals, alcohol, and other substances.

questions.question: What is the safest response to a patient with HIV/HBV coinfection who wants to stop part of ART because of pill burden?
choices: Validate the concern and coordinate promptly with HIV/hepatitis care before any regimen change
Advise a partial stop immediately
Tell the patient pill burden is not important
Change the regimen without checking HBV activity
questions.explanation: ART components may also suppress HBV. Adherence barriers deserve support, but regimen changes need coordinated planning.

questions.question: Which action best represents FNP-level viral-hepatitis care?
choices: Reconcile medications and exposures, use current guidance, coordinate specialist care, and escalate decompensation symptoms promptly
Manage all HBV and HCV treatment from memory without reference resources
Ignore co-infection testing
Treat jaundice only with lifestyle advice
questions.explanation: Safe care combines preventive counseling with current guideline use, interaction review, specialist coordination, and timely escalation.
